abstract.text:
We analyze the type of learned optimization that occurs when a learned model
(such as a neural network) is itself an optimizer—a situation we refer to as
mesa-optimization, a neologism we introduce in this paper. We believe that the
possibility of mesa-optimization raises two important questions for the safety
and transparency of advanced machine learning systems. First, under what
circumstances will learned models be optimizers, including when they should
not be? Second, when a learned model is an optimizer, what will its objective
be—how will it differ from the loss function it was trained under—and how
can it be aligned? In this paper, we provide an in-depth analysis of these two
primary questions and provide an overview of topics for future research.

evidence.quote: If pseudo-aligned mesa-optimizers may arise in advanced ML systems, as we will suggest, they could pose two critical safety problems.

thesis.text: Advanced machine learning systems may learn internal optimizers—mesa-optimizers—whose objectives can differ from the training objective, creating unintended optimization and inner alignment risks, including deceptive alignment.

As a concrete example of what a neural network optimizer might look like, consider TreeQN.[2]

Universal Planning Networks, as described by Srinivas et al.,[3] provide another example of a learned system that performs optimization, though the optimization there is built-in in the form of SGD via automatic differentiation.
For example, we might design a meta-learning system to help tune our gradient descent process.[4]

However, research such as that in Andrychowicz et al.[4] and Duan et al.[5] demonstrate that optimization algorithms can be learned by RNNs, making it possible that a Universal Planning Networks-like agent could be entirely learned—assuming a very expressive model space—including the internal optimization steps.
Previous work in this space has often centered around the concept of “optimization daemons,”[6] a framework that we believe is potentially misleading and hope to supplant.
The word mesa has been proposed as the opposite of meta.[7]

In “Scalable agent alignment via reward modeling,” Leike et al. describe the concept of the “reward-result gap” as the difference between the (in their case learned) “reward model” (what we call the base objective) and the “reward function that is recovered with perfect inverse reinforcement learning” (what we call the behavioral objective).[8]

To see this, we can think of optimization power as being measured in terms of the number of times the optimizer is able to divide the search space in half—that is, the number of bits of information provided.[9]

Indeed, our best current algorithms for those tasks involve explicitly making an optimizer (hard-coded Monte-Carlo tree search with learned heuristics) that does optimization work on the level of the learned algorithm rather than having all the optimization work done by the base optimizer.[10]

Focusing on building many individual AI services which can together offer all the capabilities of a generally-intelligent system rather than a single general-purpose artificial general intelligence (AGI), for example, might be a way to accomplish this while still remaining competitive with other approaches.[11]
Another aspect of the task that might influence the likelihood of mesa-optimization is the presence of humans in the environment.[12]

On the other hand, if a hypothetical base optimizer looks for the program with the shortest source code that solves a task, then it is more plausible that this program will itself be an optimizer.[13]

For example, architectures that explicitly give the algorithm access to a wide range of possible computations, such as recurrent neural networks or neural Turing machines,[14] seem more likely to produce mesa-optimizers.
For example, it has been shown that neural networks are more likely to fit a simple function to a set of training data, even when no regularization is used.[15]

This is closely analogous to the reason that machine learning models can fail to generalize or be susceptible to adversarial examples[19]—there are many more ways of classifying data that do well in training than any specific way the programmers had in mind.

Unidentifiability in mesa-optimization is partially analogous to the problem of unidentifiability in reward learning, in that the central issue is identifying the “correct” objective function given particular training data.[20]
Reward-predictive model-based reinforcement learning might be one possible way of accomplishing this.[21]
Iterated Distillation and Amplification might be a possible solution to problems of this form.[22]
The concept of deceptive alignment is closely related to Manheim and Garrabrant’s concept of “adversarial Goodhart.”[23]

abstract.text:
We analyze the type of learned optimization that occurs when a learned model
(such as a neural network) is itself an optimizer—a situation we refer to as
mesa-optimization, a neologism we introduce in this paper. We believe that the
possibility of mesa-optimization raises two important questions for the safety
and transparency of advanced machine learning systems. First, under what
circumstances will learned models be optimizers, including when they should
not be? Second, when a learned model is an optimizer, what will its objective
be—how will it differ from the loss function it was trained under—and how
can it be aligned? In this paper, we provide an in-depth analysis of these two
primary questions and provide an overview of topics for future research.

evidence.quote: If pseudo-aligned mesa-optimizers may arise in advanced ML systems, as we will suggest, they could pose two critical safety problems.

thesis.text: Advanced machine learning systems may learn internal optimizers—mesa-optimizers—whose objectives can differ from the training objective, creating unintended optimization and inner alignment risks, including deceptive alignment.

citations.context: For example, a bottle cap causes water to be held inside the bottle, but it is not optimizing for that outcome since it is not running any sort of optimization algorithm.[1]
As a concrete example of what a neural network optimizer might look like, consider TreeQN.[2]

Universal Planning Networks, as described by Srinivas et al.,[3] provide another example of a learned system that performs optimization, though the optimization there is built-in in the form of SGD via automatic differentiation.
For example, we might design a meta-learning system to help tune our gradient descent process.[4]

However, research such as that in Andrychowicz et al.[4] and Duan et al.[5] demonstrate that optimization algorithms can be learned by RNNs, making it possible that a Universal Planning Networks-like agent could be entirely learned—assuming a very expressive model space—including the internal optimization steps.
Previous work in this space has often centered around the concept of “optimization daemons,”[6] a framework that we believe is potentially misleading and hope to supplant.
The word mesa has been proposed as the opposite of meta.[7]

In “Scalable agent alignment via reward modeling,” Leike et al. describe the concept of the “reward-result gap” as the difference between the (in their case learned) “reward model” (what we call the base objective) and the “reward function that is recovered with perfect inverse reinforcement learning” (what we call the behavioral objective).[8]

To see this, we can think of optimization power as being measured in terms of the number of times the optimizer is able to divide the search space in half—that is, the number of bits of information provided.[9]

Indeed, our best current algorithms for those tasks involve explicitly making an optimizer (hard-coded Monte-Carlo tree search with learned heuristics) that does optimization work on the level of the learned algorithm rather than having all the optimization work done by the base optimizer.[10]
Another aspect of the task that might influence the likelihood of mesa-optimization is the presence of humans in the environment.[12]

On the other hand, if a hypothetical base optimizer looks for the program with the shortest source code that solves a task, then it is more plausible that this program will itself be an optimizer.[13]

For example, architectures that explicitly give the algorithm access to a wide range of possible computations, such as recurrent neural networks or neural Turing machines,[14] seem more likely to produce mesa-optimizers.
For example, it has been shown that neural networks are more likely to fit a simple function to a set of training data, even when no regularization is used.[15]
This suggests the following speculative conjecture: neither a minimal-depth nor minimal-size boolean circuit that solves a problem can be a mesa-optimizer.[16]

An interesting approach to analyzing this connection is presented in Ibarz et al, where empirical samples of the true reward and a learned reward on the same trajectories are used to create a scatter-plot visualization of the alignment between the two.[18]

This is closely analogous to the reason that machine learning models can fail to generalize or be susceptible to adversarial examples[19]—there are many more ways of classifying data that do well in training than any specific way the programmers had in mind.

Unidentifiability in mesa-optimization is partially analogous to the problem of unidentifiability in reward learning, in that the central issue is identifying the “correct” objective function given particular training data.[20]
Reward-predictive model-based reinforcement learning might be one possible way of accomplishing this.[21]
Iterated Distillation and Amplification might be a possible solution to problems of this form.[22]
The concept of deceptive alignment is closely related to Manheim and Garrabrant’s concept of “adversarial Goodhart.”[23]
In its most extreme form, this failure of alignment could lead to a “treacherous turn” as described by Nick Bostrom in Superintelligence.[24]
Paul Christiano provides a scenario that illustrates how deceptive alignment could pose a catastrophic risk.[25]
This situation would correspond to a mesa-optimizer that is corrigible[26] with respect to the base objective (though not necessarily the programmer’s intentions).

The mesa-optimizer is then facing a decision problem similar to the “absent-minded driver problem.”[28]
For example, in Wang et al.’s “Learning to Reinforcement Learn,” the authors claim to have produced a neural network that implements its own optimization procedure.[29]
A system is robust to distributional shift if it continues to perform well on the objective function for which it was optimized even when off the training environment.[30]
Furthermore, it has been noted in the inverse reinforcement learning literature that the reward function of an agent generally cannot be uniquely deduced from its behavior.[31]
